name: Indian standards and capacity measures (IRC:106-1990, IRC:64-1990, Indo-HCM 2017, dynamic PCU, area occupancy, LOS)
maintainer: Indian Roads Congress (IRC:106-1990 urban capacity guidelines and IRC:64-1990 rural capacity guidelines); CSIR-Central Road Research Institute (CSIR-CRRI), New Delhi, with IIT Roorkee, IIT Bombay, IIT Guwahati, SPA Delhi, SVNIT Surat, IIEST Shibpur and Anna University (Indo-HCM 2017). The area occupancy concept comes from academic work by Mallikarjuna and Ramachandra Rao (2006) and Arasan and Dhivya (2010).
first_release: IRC:64 first published 1976, revised November 1990. IRC:106 first published November 1990 (reprinted 2007 and 2016). Indo-HCM project approved October 2012; manual published by CSIR-CRRI in 2017 (executive summary dated 15 April 2014 for the draft).
last_activity: IRC:106-1990 reprint March 2016 (seen on the scanned copy). Indo-HCM 2017 is still the current edition; no 2nd edition found [uncertain].
licence: IRC codes are copyrighted publications of the Indian Roads Congress, sold by IRC; the scanned copies used here are hosted by Public.Resource.Org (law.resource.org) as Indian legal standards. Indo-HCM 2017 is a CSIR-CRRI publication; its copyright terms are not stated in the copy we read [uncertain]. Using the published numbers as model parameters or validation targets is ordinary citation and is not restricted.
code_availability: Paper only. IRC:106-1990 scanned PDF: https://law.resource.org/pub/in/bis/irc/irc.gov.in.106.1990.pdf . IRC:64-1990 scanned PDF: https://law.resource.org/pub/in/bis/irc/irc.gov.in.064.1990.pdf . Indo-HCM 2017 full text: a third-party copy at pdfcoffee.com (secondary hosting of the primary document) and a CRRI executive summary on crridom.gov.in. No software or code exists.
maintenance_health: IRC:106 has not been revised since 1990 and still uses static PCUs with only two composition bands (5% and 10%+). Indo-HCM 2017 replaced it in practice with dynamic, speed- and area-based PCUs and capacities measured in 10 metro cities. No update to Indo-HCM was found after 2017 [uncertain].
mixed_traffic_support: Both standards handle mixed traffic only by converting it to passenger car units (PCU). IRC:106-1990 (primary, read from the scanned original, Table 1) gives static urban PCUs that change with the share of that vehicle class. At 5% share / at 10% share and above: two-wheeler (motorcycle or scooter) 0.5 / 0.75; passenger car or pick-up van 1.0 / 1.0; auto-rickshaw 1.2 / 2.0; light commercial vehicle 1.4 / 2.0; truck or bus 2.2 / 3.7; agricultural tractor-trailer 4.0 / 5.0; cycle 0.4 / 0.5; cycle-rickshaw 1.5 / 2.0; tonga (horse-drawn) 1.5 / 2.0; hand cart 2.0 / 3.0. IRC:64-1990 rural PCUs (primary, Table 1): motorcycle or scooter 0.50; car, pick-up van or auto-rickshaw 1.00; agricultural tractor or LCV 1.50; truck or bus 3.00; truck-trailer or tractor-trailer 4.50; cycle 0.50; cycle-rickshaw 2.00; hand cart 3.00; horse-drawn 4.00; bullock cart 8.00 (6 for small carts). Indo-HCM 2017 uses dynamic PCU: PCU_i = (Vc/Vi) / (Ac/Ai), where Vc and Vi are the speeds of the standard car and of vehicle type i, and Ac and Ai are their projected rectangular plan areas. On urban roads the standard car area is the weighted average of small and big cars, 6.19 m2. Indo-HCM also defines a Stream Equivalency Factor Se = (flow in PCU/h) / (flow in veh/h), with regressions for urban divided roads: Se = 1 - 0.77 PTW - 0.28 PAuto + 0.53 PLCV + 2.60 PBus + 1.83 PHV - 0.66 PNMT + 12.71 (1/N), and for undivided roads: Se = 1 - 0.85 PTW - 0.31 PAuto + 0.60 PLCV + 3.09 PBus + 1.06 PHV - 1.30 PNMT - 1.29 (1/N). P terms are class shares and N is total veh/h.
non_lane_behaviour: Indo-HCM's urban chapter treats road width, not lane count, as the main design variable. Lanes are nominal (3.5 m per lane plus 0.25 m kerb shyness on each edge): 4-lane divided = 7.5 m per direction, 6-lane = 11 m, 8-lane = 14.5 m, 10-lane = 18 m, and 2-lane undivided = 7.5 m in total. Signalized-intersection saturation flow is given per metre of approach width, not per lane. The unit base saturation flow is USF0 = -60.506 W + 1137.6, which the manual rounds to 1140 - 60 W PCU/h per metre, valid for effective approach widths W of 7 to 10.5 m. Outside that range a constant USF0 applies; by continuity that would be about 720 below 7 m and about 510 above 10.5 m, but those two values are our inference and were not read in the text [uncertain]. Prevailing saturation flow is SF = W x USF0 x fbb x fbr x fis, the adjustments being for bus blockage, right-turn blockage, and initial surge or anticipation (countdown timers). Area occupancy is the concentration measure for non-lane traffic. Mallikarjuna and Rao (2006) define it as the share of time that vehicles' plan areas cover a detection zone (secondary description). A later paper writes it as ao = [sum over vehicles i of (L_i + d) x B_i / v_i] / (T x W), where L_i is vehicle length, B_i vehicle width, v_i speed, d the detection-zone length, T the observation time and W the road width (arXiv 2408.02353; this is a reproduction, not the original 2006 paper). Equivalent form: sum(t_i x a_i) / (T x A_zone), where t_i is the time vehicle i occupies the zone and a_i is its plan area. Arasan and Dhivya (2010) validated area occupancy with the HETEROSIM simulator because ordinary occupancy cannot be applied to traffic without lane discipline.
seepage_filtering_support: The standards do not model seepage explicitly. Its effect is absorbed into the low dynamic PCUs of two-wheelers: Indo-HCM median about 0.20 to 0.24 on urban midblocks, and 0.4 at signalized intersections. IRC:106 uses a static 0.5 to 0.75. Indo-HCM's signal chapter adds an initial surge / anticipation adjustment factor (fis) to saturation flow, which captures early discharge by vehicles queued ahead of the stop line.

Table 5.2 (planning use): two-wheeler range 0.10-0.31, median 0.20 (undivided) and range 0.10-0.45, median 0.22 (divided); car 1.00; bicycle range 0.34-0.50, median 0.39 (undivided) and range 0.30-0.80, median 0.42 (divided). Medians for the other classes could not be mapped reliably from the extracted text [uncertain]. Table 5.3 (evaluation, by road width), medians read in the order TW / Auto / Car / Bus / Mini bus / LCV / Two-three-axle truck / Multi-axle truck / Tractor-trailer [uncertain column mapping]: four-lane divided 0.20 / 0.80 / 1.00 / 4.58 / 2.10 / 2.30 / 3.80 / 5.10 / 5.38; six-lane divided 0.21 / 0.83 / 1.00 / 4.60 / 2.16 / 2.30 / 3.90 / 5.90 / 5.47; eight-lane divided 0.24 / 0.96 / 1.00 / 4.60 / 2.16 / 2.38 / 3.90 / 5.90 / 5.88; ten-lane divided 0.24 / 0.96 / 1.00 / 4.60 / 2.61 / 2.38 / 3.90 / 5.90. indian_calibration_evidence: BASE CAPACITIES, URBAN (Indo-HCM 2017 Table 5.4, primary text; every row checks arithmetically as lane capacity x lanes, and DSV = 0.7 x capacity). Two-lane undivided: capacity 2400 PCU/h total, 1200 PCU/h/lane, design service volume (DSV) 1680. Four-lane divided: 5400 (2700 per direction), 1350 per lane, DSV 3780 (1890 per direction). Six-lane divided: 8400 (4200 per direction), 1400 per lane, DSV 5880 (2940). Eight-lane divided: 13600 (6800), 1700 per lane, DSV 9520 (4760). Ten-lane divided: 20000 (10000), 2000 per lane, DSV 14000 (7000). The 8- and 10-lane values come from sections with 1-3 km signal spacing. Lane capacity versus car operating speed (85th percentile free speed of cars, valid for 40-80 km/h): C_lane = 20.11 V + 210.8 (Table 5.5: 55 km/h 1317; 60 km/h 1417; 65 km/h 1518; 70 km/h 1619; 75 km/h 1719 PCU/h/lane). Side-friction capacity C = C0 x FOP x FBS x FAC. The on-street parking factor is 0.70 / 0.65 / 0.40 for under 25% / 25-50% / over 50% of segment length occupied. INTERURBAN MULTILANE (Indo-HCM Ch. 3): four-lane C = 30 V + 1540 and six-lane C = 43 V + 2490 PCU/h/direction (70 km/h: 3640 and 5500; 80: 3940 and 5930; 90: 4240 and 6360; 100: 4540 and 6790). Two-lane interurban example: 2946 PCU/h for a 7.0 m carriageway with 1.5 m earthen shoulders on plain terrain. IRC:106-1990 DESIGN SERVICE VOLUMES AT LOS C (primary, Table 2, PCU/h, arterial / sub-arterial / collector): 2-lane one-way 2400 / 1900 / 1400; 2-lane two-way 1500 / 1200 / 900; 3-lane one-way 3600 / 2900 / 2200; 4-lane undivided two-way 3000 / 2400 / 1800; 4-lane divided two-way 3600 / 2900 / -; 6-lane undivided two-way 4800 / 3800 / -; 6-lane divided two-way 5400 / 4300 / -; 8-lane divided two-way 7200 / - / -. IRC:106 sets DSV at about 0.70 x capacity, so implied capacity is DSV / 0.7; for example a 4-lane divided arterial is about 5140 PCU/h (our derivation). IRC:64-1990 rural two-lane DSV at LOS B (about 0.5 x capacity), PCU/day: plain terrain 15,000 (low curvature) / 12,500 (high); rolling 11,000 / 10,000; hilly 7,000 / 5,000. Paved shoulders of at least 1.5 m add about 15%. Single-lane plain: 2000 / 1900 PCU/day.
calibration_dataset_used: Indo-HCM urban roads: base and non-base midblock sections in 10 metro cities (Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, Jaipur, Chandigarh, Surat, Ahmedabad, Thiruvananthapuram, Guwahati), recorded on video over 50-75 m traps at least 500 m from the upstream junction. Signalized intersections: 18 intersections nationwide. The raw data are not public.
calibration_method: Dynamic PCU from speed and area ratios; capacity from fitted speed-flow curves per width class; LOS bands from clustering stream speeds; Stream Equivalency regression on composition. IRC:106 and IRC:64 used committee judgement on earlier CRRI studies.
max_density_tested: Interurban 4-lane LOS F starts above 90 PCU/km/direction and 6-lane LOS F above 136 PCU/km/direction (Indo-HCM Tables 3.8 and 3.9). The urban chapter has no density threshold; urban LOS is based on speed and v/c.
validation_against_field_case: Indo-HCM worked examples, e.g. a four-lane interurban section with 1250 veh/h/direction gives 1978 PCU/h/direction, v/c = 0.56 and LOS D. No named urban junction case such as Silk Board appears in the manual.
network_import: N/A (standards define road typologies the simulator should expose: 2-lane undivided 7.5 m; 4/6/8/10-lane divided at 7.5/11/14.5/18 m per direction; signal approaches by effective width in metres).
demand_input_formats: Classified volume counts in veh/h by class, converted to PCU/h with static (IRC) or dynamic (Indo-HCM) PCU or with Se. Peak hour is about 8-10% of daily traffic in urban areas (IRC:106 clause 6.1).
data_access: IRC:106-1990 (17-page scan, 2.3 MB, scanned images needing OCR): https://law.resource.org/pub/in/bis/irc/irc.gov.in.106.1990.pdf . IRC:64-1990 (22 pages, has a text layer): https://law.resource.org/pub/in/bis/irc/irc.gov.in.064.1990.pdf . Indo-HCM 2017 full text (third-party copy): https://pdfcoffee.com/indo-hcm-2017pdf-pdf-free.html . CRRI executive summary: https://crridom.gov.in/sites/default/files/news/Development-of-Indian-Highway-Capacity-Manual-Executive-Summary-15-04-2014.pdf . No registration needed for these copies; the official Indo-HCM is sold or distributed by CSIR-CRRI [uncertain].
reuse_mode: Use as data: (1) validation targets for the capacity-versus-width test (urban lane capacity 1200-2000 PCU/h/lane; saturation flow 1140 - 60 W PCU/h/m); (2) output metrics: report dynamic PCU per class with Indo-HCM's formula from simulated speeds and plan areas, LOS from v/c using the Indo-HCM urban bands, and area occupancy computed over a virtual detection zone; (3) static IRC:106 PCU as a fallback converter for user-entered demand.
effort_within_72_hours: Low, about 3-4 hours. Hard-code a JSON table of PCU sets (IRC:106 static, Indo-HCM median), capacity targets and LOS bands; add a detector that logs per-class speed, plan area and occupancy time; compute dynamic PCU, area occupancy, v/c and LOS per link per interval. Cut: side-friction adjustment factors, interurban chapters, pedestrian chapters, and the Se regression (optional).
licence_constraint: None on our code. Cite IRC:106-1990, IRC:64-1990 and Indo-HCM (CSIR-CRRI 2017) as sources. Do not redistribute the PDFs themselves inside the app.
known_limitations: (1) Static IRC PCUs ignore speed, width and composition except for the coarse 5%/10% switch, and Indo-HCM itself says a single PCU set cannot be recommended. (2) Indo-HCM PCU ranges are wide (e.g. bus 1.79-6.5 on undivided roads), so any single number is a planning median, not a constant. (3) Base capacities are for ideal midblock sections at least 500 m from intersections with no side friction, so they are not junction capacities. (4) The 8- and 10-lane capacities come from 1-3 km signal spacing and do not transfer to dense urban grids. (5) The capacity-speed equation is valid only for 40-80 km/h operating speed. (6) The USF0 relation is valid only for 7-10.5 m approaches. (7) Our extraction of Indo-HCM Tables 5.2, 5.3, 5.6, 5.7 and 6.3 came from a scrambled PDF text layer; values whose column mapping is uncertain are flagged. (8) Indo-HCM LOS bands differ between undivided and divided roads (Table 5.6 vs 5.7). For divided urban roads: A below 0.15 v/c [uncertain], B 0.15-0.45 (83-76% of free-flow speed), C 0.46-0.75 (75-59%), D 0.76-0.85 (58-41%), E 0.86-1.00 (40-22%), F above 1.00 (below 22%). For two-lane undivided urban roads: A below 0.35 (above 89% of FFS), B 0.36-0.55, C 0.56-0.70 [uncertain, inferred from neighbours], D 0.71-0.85, E 0.86-1.00, F above 1.00. For interurban 4-lane and 6-lane: A 0-0.20, B 0.21-0.30, C 0.31-0.50, D 0.51-0.70, E 0.71-1.00, F above 1.00. Single-lane interurban: A up to 0.15, B 0.16-0.30, C 0.31-0.50, D 0.51-0.80, E 0.81-1.00, F above 1.00. IRC:106 defines LOS by speed rather than v/c: A about 90% of free-flow speed, B about 70%, C about 50%, D about 40%, E about one third, F 25-33%.
documented_failures: Using one fixed PCU set across compositions gives large errors in mixed flow. Indo-HCM introduced Se precisely because a small change in volume or composition can change PCU substantially, especially for large vehicles. Many Indian simulation papers still benchmark against IRC:106 static PCUs (e.g. WCTR 2019 comparisons of IRC, Chandra dynamic PCU and Indo-HCM), so results that agree with one method can disagree with another.
validation_approach: Indo-HCM: field speed-flow data on base sections in 10 cities; capacity from fitted speed-flow curves; LOS bands from speed clustering; worked examples. IRC:106: committee review of CRRI urban capacity studies. Our extraction was checked by OCR of the IRC:106 scan, visual inspection of the page images for Tables 1 and 2, and arithmetic checks on Indo-HCM Table 5.4 (capacity = lane capacity x lanes; DSV = 0.7 x capacity).
takeaway_for_our_build: Adopt Indo-HCM 2017 as the reference for both validation targets and output metrics, and keep IRC:106 only as a static PCU fallback. Concrete rules: (a) the capacity-versus-width test should give about 1350 PCU/h/lane on a 7.5 m directional carriageway and about 1400 on 11 m, within an explicit tolerance band (say +-20%), using Indo-HCM median PCUs to convert simulated veh/h; (b) the signal-approach discharge test should give about 1140 - 60 W PCU/h per metre of green, e.g. 720 x 7 = 5040 PCU/h for a 7 m approach and 510 x 10.5 = 5355 PCU/h for 10.5 m; (c) compute dynamic PCU_i = (Vc/Vi)/(Ac/Ai) from simulation output with a 6.19 m2 standard car, and show it next to the static IRC value so users see the difference; (d) compute area occupancy over a virtual trap as sum((L_i + d) B_i / v_i) / (T W) and use it, not veh/km, as the congestion-state variable for lane-free traffic; (e) label LOS with the Indo-HCM urban v/c bands for divided versus undivided roads, and state which table was used.
